title: Readers’ Rides: Ihor’s 2006 Nagasawa Special
content:
Maybe it’s all the recent Japan coverage, or maybe it’s the 20-year anniversary that has us nostalgic for track bikes over here. Putting that energy into the world resulted in Ihor sending in this stunning 2006 Nagasawa Special track bike, with a slick-as-shit build kit. Let’s check it out for this week’s Readers’ Rides!

I bought this frame in November 2023. I was just sitting at home, minding my own business, when I spotted this beautiful but broken Nagasawa frame on NJS Export for $150. It had a cracked seat tube near the bottom bracket. I bought it without a second thought.

It had belonged to a 2010 season champion and was originally welded in 2006. Shipping and customs fees cost twice as much as the frame itself. I already had a fork I’d bought in Japan earlier – possibly even the original one for this frame (I’m pretty sure it is).

It’s not that I needed another bike or had spare cash, but the purchase still stirred up a whirlwind of emotions. I fell instantly in love with that deep blue color. Like all glossy NJS frames, it’s hard to capture in photos – sometimes it feels like my photography skills just aren’t up to the task. Plus, the decals aren’t stickers – the lettering is stenciled on in white paint, something I hadn’t seen very often. It creates a striking contrast.

At that point, I was unemployed and had a broken frame, yet I had almost all the necessary parts at home – I was only missing a saddle and a headset. It was a situation that was both a blessing and a curse: I had everything, but I couldn’t actually build the bike. My idea was to build an NJS bike that looked like something from 2014 (I’m from Ukraine, where modern aluminum frames arrived a bit later).

I found a saddle on eBay for $30 (though shipping cost more, naturally) – brand new, in its original packaging from that era. I was absolutely thrilled because, for me, that specific saddle epitomized the bikes of 2014. Back then, my logic was simple: if you had a Fizik saddle, you were a serious road cyclist, but if you had a Zoncolan, you were just a street rider.

I bought the headset in Berlin in the summer of 2024. I just wanted to add some American-made components to the build of this Japanese bike.

I sourced all the other parts from the box where we keep our spare bike components (Yeah – I know you have a place like that). So, everything was ready – except for the frame. The seat tube needed replacing.

The moment I saw the frame, I knew exactly who I’d turn to for the repair – Dima from “Moskvich”. He handled the repair. I mailed the frame to him; he replaced the tube and sent it back.

It sounds simple enough. But in reality, Dima cut out the old tube and the old solder – while preserving the lugs – then inserted a new tube and silver-brazed it in place. NJS frame’s lugs were originally brass-brazed; they are easily repaired using silver, which has a lower melting point. When Dima finished, we saw the frame’s geometry for the first time – it turned out to have a slight sloping top tube, which pleased me even more. The journey of the frame from Dima to me took just over two months.

Just look at the quality of his work – it’s superb. The beauty and precision of his welds are amazing. As a gesture of appreciation for Dima, I also made a «МОЖНО КАТАТЬСЯ» sticker and applied it to the spot where the frame’s tubing material is usually indicated. Literally, the phrase means «Good to ride” –  Dima used to write it every time he posted on his Instagram Stories about a completed frame repair.

I had planned from the start to leave the tube and the heat-affected zones exactly as they were and simply clear-coat them. I had prepared the tube beforehand – it’s a heat-treated Kaisei tube sold by the guys from Rene Herse. Nagasawa seat tubes usually feature Italian and Japanese flag decals. I didn’t have any on hand, and without them, the “Nagasawa” lettering looked a bit lonely.

So, I photographed the logo from the down tube, scaled it up exactly twofold, and printed some stickers. The size of the lettering ended up matching the seat tube’s circumference almost perfectly – falling just two millimeters short. To me, those bold, oversized letters are a fundamental element of Japanese visual culture.

I didn’t want to go into too much detail, as that would spoil the bike’s simplicity. (If anyone is interested, I can send it via PM.) Overall, the bike is a simple build, as it’s meant for daily city riding. There’s nothing ultra-rare or collectible on it – except, perhaps, for the black SUGINO Super Zen chainring, which is nearly impossible to find these days.

But the bike is special to me because it incorporates some of my absolute favorite components that had otherwise been sitting unused. The old black pedals have faded in the sun, and their shade now matches the chainring perfectly. These are my very first Toshi double straps – they’ve been through it all with me since, I think, 2012.

For me, there is probably nothing worse than something built solely for the sake of building, without ever actually being used. After all, the true beauty of a mechanism lies in its operation. I finished this bike in February 2025. In a few months, I’ll have been riding it for two years, and it brings me joy every time I take it out. I really hope that feeling only grows stronger with each passing year.

The bike looks a bit different now – I’ve installed 25mm tires and a small basket. I might post a photo on my Instagram later. Thanks to everyone who read this article. Peace!

Build Spec:

  • Frame/Fork/ NAGASAWA SPECIAL 2006/NAGASAWA
  • Headset: Chris King GripNut
  • Crankset/Bottom Bracket: Dura-Ace 7600/ Sugino 75
  • Pedals/Straps: MKS Custom Nuevo / TOSHI double straps
  • Cog/Chainring/Chain: EuroAsia Gold 16T / Sugino Super ZEN 46t / DID
  • Handlebars/Stem/Bar Tape: Civia Emerson 46cm / Cinelli 1A 90mm / ENVE
  • Saddle/Seatpost: Selle San Marco Zoncolan / ENVE
  • Front Wheel/Hub/Tire: HED Belgium R / Dura-Ace / Continental Gatorskin 23mm
  • Rear Wheel/Hub/Tire: HED Belgium R / Dura-Ace / Continental  Gatorskin 23mm
  • Additional: Nitto Bottle Cage / Kashimax Frame Protector
